Lessons.Title: Modeling with Systems of Inequalities in Two Variables
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning objective: choose variables and meaningful units, build and interpret a multi-constraint linear model, and evaluate competing feasible solutions, including boundary and physical restrictions. First-party Edulytiks adaptation of Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition U02:L26, https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/2/26/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0). This culminates in a student-authored model rather than a predefined one-number answer. Publisher Addressing HSA-CED.A.3, HSA-REI.D.12 and HSN-Q.A.2.

Original hypothetical trail mix design: produce exactly 1,000 grams from nut mix x grams and fruit mix y grams, with per-gram nutritional estimates nut protein 0.20 g and fruit 0.03 g, and costs $0.006/g and $0.004/g respectively. Require at least 100 g protein and no more than $5.20 total cost, with x,y≥0. System: x+y=1000, 0.20x+0.03y≥100, 0.006x+0.004y≤5.20. These numbers are fabricated for a safe mathematical simulation, not real nutrition advice or product labels.

Substitute y=1000−x. Protein: 0.20x+0.03(1000−x)≥100 implies 0.17x≥70, so x≥70/0.17≈411.765 g. Cost: 0.006x+0.004(1000−x)≤5.20 implies 4+0.002x≤5.20, so x≤600 g. Any x in [411.765,600], with y=1000−x, meets these simplified constraints. For real-world mixing specify measurement precision, allergies and nutritional data quality.

Candidate x=500,y=500 gives protein 0.2×500+0.03×500=115 g and price $3+$2=$5.00, feasible. Candidate x=400,y=600 gives protein 80+18=98 g, below requirement; x=700,y=300 gives price $4.20+$1.20=$5.40, above budget. The exact permissible mixture depends on actual verified labels and intended units.

Student task: propose a different two-ingredient original model with at least three inequalities/equalities, find and explain its feasible region, check one boundary point and one invalid point and critique the sensitivity to changed per-unit parameters. Teacher-scored rubric (0–2 each, total 8): meaningful variables and source assumptions, accurate constraints/domains, calculated feasible region, and evidence-backed model evaluation and limitations. Never pretend to have prepared or tasted trail mix.

KeyConcepts.Title: Model construction
KeyConcepts.Definition: A mathematical model selects quantities, assumptions and constraints from a situation.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Write variables and units before coefficients.

KeyConcepts.Title: Feasible interval
KeyConcepts.Definition: Multiple linear restrictions can leave a bounded interval of admissible mixtures.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Eliminate one variable and intersect every bound.

KeyConcepts.Title: Parameter sensitivity
KeyConcepts.Definition: Feasibility can change if measured ingredient properties or budget change.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Explain that coefficients are assumptions and must be validated in reality.
KeyConcepts.Example: A $5.20 limit caps nut mix at 600 g with the chosen costs.

WorkedExamples.Title: Derive protein lower bound
WorkedExamples.Question: Find the nut mix x needed for ≥100 g protein in 1000 g total.
WorkedExamples.Method: Interpret the stated inequality system, use valid domains and independently verify each numerical case.
Steps: Divide positive 0.17 to obtain x≥70/0.17≈411.765 g.
WorkedExamples.Answer: At least about 411.765 g nut mix is required.
WorkedExamples.Check: At x=400, protein 98 g and fails.

WorkedExamples.Title: Derive budget upper bound
WorkedExamples.Question: Find x meeting total cost ≤$5.20.
WorkedExamples.Method: Interpret the stated inequality system, use valid domains and independently verify each numerical case.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Nut mix must not exceed 600 g in this model.

WorkedExamples.Title: Check feasible and invalid recipes
WorkedExamples.Question: Compare (500,500), (400,600) and (700,300) grams.
WorkedExamples.Method: Interpret the stated inequality system, use valid domains and independently verify each numerical case.
Steps: For 500/500, protein 100+15=115 g and cost $3+$2=$5; feasible.
For 400/600, protein 80+18=98 g<100; protein requirement fails.
Every pair meets mass 1000 g, but only the first meets all constraints.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Only (500,500) is feasible among the three.
WorkedExamples.Check: Check each inequality independently; total mass alone is insufficient.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating fictional coefficients as real nutritional labels
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The lesson's numbers are mathematical assumptions, not medical/nutrition advice.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Label the model as simulated and verify real data separately.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Keeping only one constraint in the feasible set
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Meeting protein while exceeding cost is still invalid.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Intersect total mass, protein, cost and nonnegative bounds.

SummaryPoints: A complete model includes variables, domains, quantified assumptions and multiple constraints.
The simplified trail mix has permissible nut grams approximately 411.765–600.
The 500/500 blend satisfies mass, protein and cost in this fictional setting.
Model construction and evaluation require teacher judgement and honest data provenance.

Visuals.Description: First-party mathematical examples with explicit limits, excluding publisher graphics and any unobserved real survey or product data.
